t: Number of Valid Words in a Sentence — Token Validation Made Precise
o: The sentence mixes lowercase letters, digits, hyphens, the punctuation marks ! . , , and spaces. Tokens are separated by ONE OR MORE spaces, and a token is a valid word only if it contains no digits, has at most one hyphen placed strictly between two lowercase letters, and has at most one punctuation mark sitting at the very end. We simply inspect each token against these three rules and count survivors. In Example 1, "cat", "and" and "dog" all pass, so the answer is 3. In Example 2, "!this" fails because punctuation leads the token, while "1-s" and "b8d!" fail on digits — answer 0. In Example 3, "stone-game10" is disqualified by digits and the five plain words pass. Constraints bound the sentence at 1000 characters, so any single linear scan over tokens is far more than fast enough.
k: Split on runs of whitespace: consecutive or leading/trailing spaces mean a naive single-space split creates phantom empty tokens.
A digit anywhere disqualifies a token immediately; otherwise enforce the hyphen rule (flanked by letters on both sides) and the punctuation rule (at most one, last character only).
Everything is O(n): each character is examined a constant number of times.

a.n: Approach 1: Scan Each Token Character by Character
a.i: Split the sentence on whitespace and validate each token independently: reject any digit; allow a hyphen only once and only when both immediate neighbors exist and are lowercase letters; allow ! . or , only as the final character. Summing the tokens that survive gives the answer.
s: Split the sentence into tokens on whitespace.
For each token, scan its characters left to right.
Reject the token if any digit appears.
Count hyphens: more than one, a hyphen at either end, or a hyphen next to a non-letter rejects the token.
Reject when ! . or , appears anywhere except the last position; count the accepted tokens.
a.t: O(n) — every character of the sentence is inspected a constant number of times.
a.sp: O(n) — the split materializes all tokens; the scan itself uses O(1) extra.

a.n: Approach 2: Regex Full Match per Token
a.i: The three rules collapse into one pattern: letters optionally joined by a single internal hyphen, optionally followed by one trailing punctuation mark — or a lone punctuation mark. A token is valid exactly when the pattern matches the entire token, eliminating all manual index bookkeeping.
s: Count tokens that are fully matched by the pattern.
a.t: O(n) — the pattern has no ambiguous repetition, so matching each token is linear in its length.
a.sp: O(n) — token storage dominates; the compiled pattern is constant-size.

w: Prefer Approach 1 in an interview unless regexes are welcomed: it is transparent, easy to debug, and adapts instantly to rule changes. Pitfalls: forgetting repeated spaces (empty tokens must not be counted), accepting a hyphen beside punctuation or at a token edge, and allowing punctuation mid-token. Worth testing: a lone "." (valid), "a-b-c" (two hyphens, invalid), "a-," (punctuation not last, invalid). Likely follow-ups: extend the alphabet (capitals, apostrophes, accents) — Approach 1 absorbs each with one extra condition, while the regex needs a rewrite.
